title: Histories
creator: herodotus
location: Written in Greece and southern Italy; earliest complete manuscripts medieval (e.g. Laurentian Library, Florence)
note: The first great work of Western history: an inquiry into the origins and course of the Persian Wars, ranging across the peoples of the known world.
description: Herodotus composed his Histories in the third quarter of the fifth century BC, probably performing parts of it aloud before it took its final form; later scholars divided it into nine books, each named after a Muse. The first half travels outward, describing the rise of Persia and the customs, geography and wonders of Lydia, Egypt, Scythia and other lands, often in long digressions. The second half narrows to the invasions of Greece by Darius and Xerxes, culminating in Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea. Herodotus compares competing oral accounts, admits uncertainty and searches for causes in human motives as well as divine retribution. His word historia, meaning inquiry, gave history its name, and his combination of narrative, ethnography and analysis set the agenda for the discipline.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War
creator: thucydides
location: Written in Athens and in exile; medieval manuscripts (e.g. Laurentian Library, Florence)
note: A contemporary analysis of the great war between Athens and Sparta, famous for its rigour and its speeches on power and justice.
description: Thucydides began writing at the outbreak of the war in 431 BC, convinced it would be the greatest conflict the Greeks had known. His account, divided by later editors into eight books, follows the war year by year, summer and winter, until it breaks off in 411 BC. He explains his method at the outset: he checked eyewitness reports and composed speeches to convey what the situation demanded. Set pieces include Pericles' Funeral Oration, the plague of Athens, the civil war at Corcyra, the Melian Dialogue, in which Athenian envoys tell the weak that they must suffer what they must, and the catastrophic expedition to Sicily. The work became a model of political history and a foundational text for theorists of international relations, from Hobbes, who translated it, to modern realists.

title: Anabasis
creator: xenophon
location: Written in Greece (probably at Scillus, near Olympia)
note: Xenophon's account of the 'march up country' of ten thousand Greek mercenaries into Persia and their retreat to the sea.
description: The Anabasis tells how Cyrus the Younger hired Greek mercenaries in 401 BC to seize the Persian throne from his brother, how Cyrus was killed at Cunaxa near Babylon, and how the stranded Greeks, their generals murdered, elected new leaders, among them Xenophon himself, and fought their way north through the mountains of Kurdistan and Armenia to the Black Sea. The moment when the soldiers sight the sea and cry 'Thalatta! Thalatta!' is among the most famous scenes in ancient literature. Xenophon wrote in the third person and published the work under another name, perhaps to make it seem impartial. Its plain style made it a standard schoolbook, and its picture of a democratic army improvising its survival has fascinated soldiers and writers ever since.

title: Hellenica
creator: xenophon
location: Written in Greece
note: A history of Greece from 411 to 362 BC, continuing Thucydides from where he broke off.
description: The Hellenica begins abruptly where Thucydides' history ends, in 411 BC, and carries the story through the end of the Peloponnesian War, the Spartan hegemony and the rise of Thebes, ending with the battle of Mantinea in 362 BC. Xenophon wrote as a participant in some events and with obvious sympathy for Sparta and its king Agesilaus, and he passes over some important developments, such as the founding of the Second Athenian League, in near silence. Even so, it is the only continuous contemporary narrative of the period to survive, and its vivid scenes, such as the trial of the generals after Arginusae, make it indispensable.

title: Histories
creator: polybius
location: Written in Rome and Greece; books 1–5 survive complete in medieval manuscripts
note: A universal history explaining how Rome conquered the Mediterranean world between the First Punic War and 146 BC.
description: Polybius asked a question he thought no one could ignore: how and under what kind of government the Romans had brought nearly the whole inhabited world under their rule in less than fifty-three years. To answer it he wrote a history linking events in Italy, Greece, Africa and Asia, which he saw as having become a single interconnected story. The surviving books cover the Punic Wars and Hannibal's invasion of Italy in detail, and book 6 contains his famous analysis of the Roman constitution as a balance of consuls, Senate and people. He set out strict principles for historians, insisting on personal inquiry, knowledge of geography and politics, and impartiality. His theory of mixed government passed through Cicero and Machiavelli to Montesquieu and the American founders.

title: Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico)
creator: julius-caesar
type: War commentary (7 books, plus an 8th by Hirtius)
location: Written in Gaul and Rome
note: Caesar's own account of his conquest of Gaul, in clear third-person prose that doubled as political propaganda.
description: Caesar wrote seven books of commentaries covering his campaigns in Gaul from 58 to 52 BC, probably sending them to Rome year by year or publishing them together around 51 BC, while his enemies in the Senate attacked his conduct. An eighth book was added after his death by his officer Aulus Hirtius. The work opens with the famous statement that all Gaul is divided into three parts, and describes his wars against the Helvetii, the Belgae and the Germans, two expeditions to Britain, and the great revolt led by Vercingetorix that ended at the siege of Alesia. Its descriptions of Gallic and Germanic society are among the earliest we have. Its plain, controlled style presents Caesar's actions as necessary and successful, and it has long served as a primer of Latin and of military history.

title: Commentaries on the Civil War (De Bello Civili)
creator: julius-caesar
location: Written in Italy and on campaign
note: Caesar's account of the first years of his civil war against Pompey and the Senate, from the Rubicon to Pharsalus.
description: The Civil War covers the years 49 and 48 BC: Caesar's invasion of Italy, his campaigns in Spain, the siege of Massilia, the war in Greece culminating in the battle of Pharsalus and Pompey's flight to Egypt, where he was murdered. Caesar presents himself as a moderate, merciful leader forced to defend his dignity and the rights of the tribunes against a narrow faction, and his opponents as arrogant and divided. The work is unfinished and may not have been published in his lifetime. It is a key source for the fall of the Roman Republic and a classic example of political self-justification.

title: The Conspiracy of Catiline (Bellum Catilinae)
creator: sallust
location: Written in Rome
note: A short, dramatic account of Catiline's attempted coup in 63 BC, used to diagnose the moral corruption of the Republic.
description: Sallust's first monograph tells how the bankrupt aristocrat Lucius Sergius Catilina plotted to seize power in Rome in 63 BC, and how the consul Cicero exposed the conspiracy, leading to the execution of several conspirators without trial and Catiline's death in battle. Sallust frames the story with a meditation on how Rome's virtue was corrupted by wealth and ambition after the fall of Carthage. The centrepiece is a pair of speeches in the Senate debate on the conspirators' fate by Julius Caesar, urging clemency, and Cato the Younger, demanding death. The work is notable for giving Cicero less credit than he gave himself. It became a model of compact political history.

title: The Jugurthine War (Bellum Jugurthinum)
creator: sallust
location: Written in Rome
note: Sallust's account of Rome's war against the Numidian king Jugurtha, a story of aristocratic corruption and popular anger.
description: This monograph narrates the war of 112–105 BC against Jugurtha, a ruthless prince who seized the throne of Numidia in North Africa and repeatedly bribed Roman senators and commanders. Sallust chose the subject, he said, because it was the first time the arrogance of the nobility was challenged. The war was finally won by Gaius Marius, a 'new man' from outside the aristocracy, with the help of his quaestor Sulla, whose later rivalry would plunge Rome into civil war. The work combines geography of Africa, battle narrative and speeches, and was much read by Renaissance and early-modern writers on politics.

title: History of Rome (Ab Urbe Condita)
creator: livy
location: Written in Rome; medieval manuscripts, e.g. the 5th-century Codex Puteaneus (Bibliothèque nationale de France)
note: Livy's monumental history of Rome from its foundation to 9 BC, the source of the classic stories of the early Republic.
description: Livy spent some forty years writing a history of Rome 'from the founding of the city', running to 142 books and ending with the death of Augustus' stepson Drusus in 9 BC. Only books 1–10 and 21–45 survive, covering the city's legendary origins to 293 BC and the period from Hannibal's war to the conquest of Macedon in 167 BC; the rest are known through summaries. In his preface Livy invites readers to study the lives and morals that made Rome great and the decline that followed. His stories of Romulus and Remus, Horatius at the bridge, Lucretia, Cincinnatus and Hannibal's crossing of the Alps became the common stock of European culture. Renaissance humanists sought lost books eagerly, Petrarch assembled a text, and Machiavelli built his political philosophy on a commentary on the first ten books.

title: Annals
creator: tacitus
location: Written in Rome; books 1–6 survive in a single 9th-century manuscript (Laurentian Library, Florence)
note: Tacitus' history of Rome from the death of Augustus to Nero, a dark and brilliant study of power under the early emperors.
description: The Annals cover the Julio-Claudian emperors from Tiberius to Nero, AD 14 to 68, though the books on Caligula, the early years of Claudius and Nero's last years are lost. Tacitus arranges the narrative year by year in the old republican manner, while showing how real power had passed to the emperor and his household. Famous passages include the treason trials under Tiberius, the death of Germanicus, the revolt of Boudica in Britain, Nero's murder of his mother Agrippina, and the great fire of Rome, after which Nero blamed the Christians, the earliest non-Christian account of their persecution. The surviving books depend on two medieval manuscripts in Florence. Tacitus' irony and moral intensity made the Annals a handbook for critics of tyranny from the Renaissance onward.

title: Histories
creator: tacitus
location: Written in Rome; survives in the second Medicean manuscript (Laurentian Library, Florence)
note: Tacitus' history of the civil wars of AD 69, the 'year of the four emperors', and the Flavian dynasty.
description: The Histories originally covered the years from 69 to the death of Domitian in 96, but only the first four books and part of the fifth survive, covering 69 and 70. They describe a terrible year in which Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian successively seized power, with armies marching on Rome and the Capitol burned. Tacitus reveals what he calls the secret of empire: that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome. The surviving part ends with the revolt of the Batavians on the Rhine and the opening of the siege of Jerusalem. It is one of the most gripping narratives of political collapse in ancient literature.

title: Germania
creator: tacitus
location: Written in Rome; a manuscript rediscovered at Hersfeld and brought to Rome c. 1455
note: A short treatise on the lands and peoples of Germany beyond the Rhine, later seized upon by German nationalists.
description: In the Germania Tacitus describes the geography, customs, religion and tribes of the Germanic peoples beyond the Roman frontier. Drawing on earlier writers and perhaps on traders and soldiers, he portrays them as fierce, free and unspoiled, implicitly contrasting their simplicity with Roman luxury, though he also notes drunkenness and idleness. The text survived through a single medieval manuscript rediscovered in the fifteenth century, after which German humanists used it to claim a noble ancient ancestry. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries it was distorted to support racial nationalism, including by the Nazis, which led the classicist Arnaldo Momigliano to count it among the most dangerous books ever written. Scholars today read it as a Roman text about Roman concerns.

title: Agricola
creator: tacitus
location: Written in Rome
note: Tacitus' tribute to his father-in-law Agricola, governor of Britain, and a key source for Roman Britain.
description: The Agricola is a short biography of Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the general who governed Britain from about 77 to 84 and led Roman armies into Scotland, defeating the Caledonians at Mons Graupius. Written after the death of Domitian, it praises Agricola as a good man who served honourably under a bad emperor, and it includes a speech put into the mouth of the Caledonian leader Calgacus attacking Roman imperialism with the famous charge that they make a desert and call it peace. It is the most detailed ancient account of Britain and its conquest.

title: Lives of the Caesars
creator: suetonius
location: Written in Rome; oldest surviving manuscript 9th century
note: Biographies of Julius Caesar and the first eleven emperors, rich in personal detail, anecdote and scandal.
description: Suetonius wrote the Lives of the Caesars while working in Hadrian's administration, dedicating them to the praetorian prefect Septicius Clarus. The twelve lives run from Julius Caesar to Domitian. Rather than following a strict chronological narrative, Suetonius organises each life by themes: family, career, public works, character, appearance, habits, omens and death. He quotes letters of Augustus and other documents from the imperial archives, along with rumours and gossip that make the book memorable and controversial. Medieval writers such as Einhard used it as a model, and it remains essential for the study of the early empire, and the popular image of Caligula and Nero owes much to it.

title: Parallel Lives
creator: plutarch
location: Written in Chaeronea, Greece
note: Paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans, compared for their virtues and vices, which taught Europe its picture of ancient heroes.
description: The Parallel Lives consist of twenty-three surviving pairs of biographies, each linking a Greek and a Roman, such as Alexander and Caesar, Demosthenes and Cicero, or Theseus and Romulus, most followed by a short comparison, plus four single lives. Plutarch explained that he was writing lives, not histories, and that a small action, a phrase or a jest often reveals character better than battles. His aim was moral: to offer examples to imitate and to avoid. Translated into French by Jacques Amyot in 1559 and into English by Thomas North in 1579, the Lives became one of the most influential books of the Renaissance. Shakespeare took the plots of his Roman plays from North's translation, and the American and French revolutionaries drew republican models from it.

title: The Jewish War
creator: josephus
location: Written in Rome
note: An eyewitness history of the Jewish revolt against Rome of AD 66–73, including the destruction of Jerusalem and the fall of Masada.
description: Josephus first wrote an account of the war in Aramaic for the peoples of the East and then produced a Greek version, the one that survives, in Rome in the 70s. After a long introduction covering Jewish history from the Maccabees, it tells how the revolt broke out, how Josephus himself commanded in Galilee and surrendered, and how Titus besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple in AD 70, with horrific scenes of famine and slaughter. It ends with the siege of Masada, where, according to Josephus, the defenders chose mass suicide rather than capture. He blames the disaster on a minority of extremists and treats the Romans as instruments of God's will, an interpretation shaped by his position. The work is the main source for these events and was read for centuries alongside the Bible.

title: Antiquities of the Jews
creator: josephus
location: Written in Rome
note: A history of the Jewish people from the Creation to the eve of the revolt against Rome, written for a Greek-speaking audience.
description: In the twenty books of the Antiquities, completed around 93 or 94, Josephus retold the history of the Jews from the creation of the world, following the Hebrew Bible, through the Persian, Hellenistic and Hasmonean periods to the reign of Herod the Great and the Roman governors of Judaea. He wrote to present his people's laws and traditions as ancient and admirable to Greek and Roman readers. For the period after the Bible he is often the only source, preserving decrees and documents. The work contains brief references to John the Baptist and James, the brother of Jesus, and the Testimonium Flavianum on Jesus, generally believed to contain Christian additions. Christians preserved and copied the Antiquities throughout the Middle Ages.

title: Anabasis of Alexander
creator: arrian
location: Written in the Roman East or Athens
note: The most reliable ancient account of Alexander the Great's campaigns, based on lost memoirs by his companions.
description: Arrian's Anabasis of Alexander, named after Xenophon's work, follows Alexander from his accession in 336 BC through the conquest of the Persian Empire, the campaigns in Central Asia and India, and the return to Babylon, where he died in 323 BC. Arrian explains that he relied principally on Ptolemy, Alexander's general and later king of Egypt, and on Aristobulus, an engineer on the expedition, because both had taken part and wrote after Alexander's death, when they had less reason to flatter him. He clearly marks other material as hearsay. Though admiring, he criticises Alexander's excesses, such as the killing of Cleitus. Because the contemporary sources are lost, Arrian is the foundation of most modern narratives of Alexander.

title: Res Gestae (History)
creator: ammianus
location: Written in Rome
note: The last great Latin history of the Roman Empire, ending with the Gothic victory at Adrianople in 378.
description: Ammianus wrote his history in Rome in the late 380s and early 390s, continuing Tacitus from the reign of Nerva. The first thirteen books are lost; the surviving books 14 to 31 cover the years 353 to 378 in great detail, drawing on his own experience as a staff officer. Highlights include the siege of Amida, which he escaped, the career of the emperor Julian, whom he admired, the arrival of the Huns, and the catastrophic defeat and death of the emperor Valens at Adrianople. He includes digressions on geography, science and the vices of the Roman aristocracy and populace. Writing as a pagan in a Christian empire, he is generally fair-minded. Gibbon relied on him heavily.

title: Ecclesiastical History
creator: eusebius
location: Written in Caesarea, Palestine
note: The first history of the Christian Church, from Christ to the victory of Constantine, built on quoted documents.
description: Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History, which he revised several times before reaching its final form around 324, traces the Church from the time of Christ through the succession of bishops in the great sees, the lives of Christian writers, the struggles against heresy, the sufferings of the Jews and the persecutions of Christians, to the triumph of Constantine. Unlike classical historians, Eusebius quoted his sources at length, so that his work preserves extracts from many early Christian writings that are otherwise lost. It created a new genre, church history, imitated by Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret and, centuries later, Bede. Modern scholars use it with care, as it is shaped by Eusebius' theological views and his celebration of a Christian empire.

title: Life of Constantine
creator: eusebius
location: Written in Caesarea, Palestine
note: Eusebius' admiring account of the first Christian emperor, including the vision of the cross before the Milvian Bridge.
description: Written after Constantine's death in 337 and left unfinished at Eusebius' own death in 339, the Life of Constantine praises the emperor as God's chosen servant. It reports Constantine's own account, told to Eusebius under oath, of seeing a cross of light in the sky with the words 'by this, conquer' before his victory over Maxentius in 312. It describes his church-building, the Council of Nicaea and his laws, quoting many imperial letters. The authenticity of these documents was once doubted but is now largely accepted, while the work as a whole is read as a panegyric rather than a balanced biography. It shaped the medieval image of the Christian ruler.

title: History of the Wars
creator: procopius
location: Written in Constantinople
note: Procopius' eyewitness history of Justinian's wars against Persia, the Vandals and the Goths.
description: The Wars recount the campaigns of the emperor Justinian, mostly led by Belisarius, in three parts: against the Sasanian Persians in the east, against the Vandal kingdom in North Africa, and against the Ostrogoths in Italy, followed by an eighth book bringing events up to 553. Procopius, writing in classicising Greek modelled on Herodotus and Thucydides, was present at many of the events as Belisarius' secretary. The work includes a famous description of the Nika riots of 532, in which Theodora is said to have persuaded Justinian not to flee, and the first clear account of the bubonic plague that struck Constantinople in 542. It is the principal narrative source for the age of Justinian.

title: Secret History
creator: procopius
location: Written in Constantinople; unpublished in antiquity, rediscovered in the Vatican Library and first printed in 1623
note: Procopius' private, scandalous attack on Justinian, Theodora and Belisarius, published long after his death.
description: The Secret History, whose Greek title Anekdota means 'unpublished things', was written around 550 as a hidden companion to the Wars. In it Procopius claims to reveal what he could not write openly: that Justinian was a demon in human form who ruined the empire with taxes and wars, that the empress Theodora had been a notorious actress and prostitute, and that Belisarius was dominated by his wife Antonina. The work was known in Byzantium but rediscovered in the West only in the seventeenth century, when its first editor printed it from a Vatican manuscript in 1623. Historians have long debated how to reconcile its venom with the official praise of the Buildings. It remains a fascinating and much-quoted source, used with caution.

title: History of the Franks (Ten Books of Histories)
creator: gregory-of-tours
location: Written in Tours, Gaul
note: The chief source for Merovingian Gaul, full of kings' feuds, bishops' quarrels and miracles.
description: Gregory called his work simply the Ten Books of Histories; the title History of the Franks was added later. It begins with the Creation and a summary of world history, but from the fifth book onward it describes Gregory's own time in great detail: the struggles between the sons and grandsons of Clovis, the feud between queens Brunhild and Fredegund, plagues, famines and portents, and the day-to-day affairs of the Church. Clovis's conversion and baptism, told in book 2, became a founding moment in French national memory. Gregory writes as a bishop interpreting events morally, and he often appears in his own pages. Without him the history of sixth-century Gaul would be almost unknown.

title: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
creator: bede
location: Written at Jarrow, Northumbria; early copies include the St Petersburg Bede and the Moore Bede (Cambridge University Library)
note: Bede's history of Christianity among the English, the foundation of early English history and a model of careful scholarship.
description: Bede completed the Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum in 731. It runs from Caesar's invasion of Britain to Bede's own day, focusing on the conversion of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms by missionaries from Rome and from Ireland and Iona, the decision at the Synod of Whitby in 664 to follow Roman customs, and the lives of saints such as Aidan and Cuthbert. In his preface Bede names the people who supplied him with information, and he quotes letters and documents, an unusual practice that makes his work exceptionally valuable. Memorable passages include Pope Gregory's pun on Angles and angels and the image of human life as a sparrow flying through a lighted hall. Bede's use of anno Domini dating helped spread the system. Two manuscripts copied within a few years of his death survive.

title: Life of Charlemagne (Vita Karoli Magni)
creator: einhard
location: Written in the Frankish Empire (Aachen or Seligenstadt)
note: A courtier's portrait of Charlemagne, modelled on Suetonius, and the first secular biography of the Middle Ages.
description: Einhard wrote his Life of Charlemagne some years after the emperor's death in 814; its exact date is debated. Following the structure of Suetonius' lives, especially that of Augustus, it describes Charlemagne's wars against the Saxons, Lombards and Avars, his building works and his coronation as emperor in Rome in 800, and then his family, appearance, habits and death. Einhard records that the king tried to learn to write late in life, keeping tablets under his pillow, but without success. It is an idealised portrait, but by someone who knew him well, and it shaped the image of Charlemagne for the rest of the Middle Ages. More than eighty medieval manuscripts survive.

title: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
creator: anglo-saxon-chroniclers
location: Compiled in Wessex and continued in several English monasteries; manuscripts in the British Library, Bodleian Library, and Corpus Christi College, Cambridge
note: A year-by-year record of English history in Old English, from the Roman era to 1154.
description: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a collection of annals in Old English, first compiled in the 890s in Wessex, probably in the circle of King Alfred, drawing on Bede and earlier records. Copies were distributed to monasteries and continued independently, so the nine surviving manuscripts and fragments differ. Entries range from a single sentence to long narratives of Alfred's wars with the Vikings, the reign of Æthelred the Unready and the Norman Conquest. The Peterborough Chronicle, continued until 1154, gives a bitter account of the anarchy of King Stephen's reign. As the first continuous history of a European people written in its own vernacular, it is a key source both for history and for the development of the English language.

title: Bayeux Tapestry
creator: bayeux-tapestry-makers
type: Embroidered narrative (wool on linen, c. 70 m)
location: Bayeux Museum (Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux), Normandy
note: A 70-metre embroidered strip telling the story of the Norman Conquest of England, from Harold's oath to the battle of Hastings.
description: Though called a tapestry, it is an embroidery in coloured wools on linen, about 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, probably made in England in the decade after the Conquest for Bishop Odo of Bayeux. In some fifty scenes with Latin captions it shows Harold Godwinson's journey to Normandy and his oath to Duke William, the death of Edward the Confessor and Harold's coronation, Halley's comet, William's preparations and Channel crossing, and the battle of Hastings in 1066, ending with Harold's death and the flight of the English; the end is lost. Its borders contain fables, animals and scenes of daily life. It is a unique visual source for armour, ships, horses and buildings of the eleventh century, and its version of events largely justifies the Norman claim. It has been displayed in Bayeux for most of its history.

title: Domesday Book
creator: william-the-conqueror
location: The National Archives, Kew, London
note: The great survey of the lands and resources of England ordered by William the Conqueror, the most complete record of any medieval kingdom.
description: At Christmas 1085 William ordered commissioners to survey every shire in England, recording who held each estate before and after the Conquest, how many ploughs, people, mills, woods and animals it contained, and what it was worth. The returns were compiled in 1086 into two volumes, Great Domesday and Little Domesday, covering most of England, though not London, Winchester or the far north. The name Domesday, meaning day of judgement, was given later because its verdicts could not be appealed. It shows the near-total replacement of the English landholding class by Normans. It was used as legal evidence for centuries and is still consulted by historians, geographers and place-name scholars; it is kept at the National Archives in Kew.

title: Alexiad
creator: anna-komnene
location: Written in Constantinople
note: A Byzantine princess's history of her father Alexios I's reign, with a unique Byzantine view of the First Crusade.
description: Anna Komnene wrote the Alexiad in the 1140s, in retirement in a convent in Constantinople, in a learned Greek modelled on classical historians. Its fifteen books tell the story of the reign of her father Alexios I Komnenos from 1081 to 1118: his rise to power, his wars against the Norman Robert Guiscard and his son Bohemond, against the Pechenegs and the Seljuk Turks, and the arrival of the armies of the First Crusade in 1096–97, whose leaders she describes with a mixture of admiration and suspicion. Anna names her sources, including her own memories and old soldiers' accounts, and repeatedly insists on her impartiality while plainly idealising her father. It is a major source for Byzantine history and the crusades, and a landmark of historical writing by a woman.

title: History of the Kings of Britain (Historia Regum Britanniae)
creator: geoffrey-of-monmouth
location: Written in Oxford; over 200 medieval manuscripts survive
note: A pseudo-history of British kings from the Trojan Brutus to the seventh century that launched the legend of King Arthur.
description: Geoffrey of Monmouth claimed to have translated a very ancient book in the British language given to him by Walter, archdeacon of Oxford, though most scholars believe this is a fiction covering his own invention combined with material from earlier chronicles and Welsh tradition. The Historia describes the founding of Britain by Brutus, great-grandson of Aeneas, a long line of kings including Lear and Cymbeline, the prophecies of Merlin, and above all the reign of Arthur, who defeats the Saxons and conquers much of Europe before being betrayed by Mordred. Some medieval critics dismissed it as fable, but it became enormously popular and was accepted as history by many for centuries. It provided material for Arthurian romance, for Shakespeare and Spenser, and for royal propaganda.

title: Magna Carta
creator: english-barons-1215
location: Four original 1215 exemplifications survive: two in the British Library, one each at Lincoln Castle and Salisbury Cathedral
note: The charter of liberties agreed by King John at Runnymede in 1215, which became a symbol of the rule of law and of limits on power.
description: Magna Carta, the Great Charter, was granted by King John at Runnymede in June 1215 as a peace settlement with rebellious barons. Its sixty-three clauses addressed specific grievances about feudal dues, inheritance, the rights of the church, justice and the royal forests, and set up a council of twenty-five barons to enforce it. Most famously, it promised that no free man would be imprisoned or deprived of his rights except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land, and that justice would not be sold, denied or delayed. The charter was annulled by the pope within weeks, but reissued in revised form in 1216, 1217 and 1225 and became part of English law. Seventeenth-century parliamentarians invoked it against the Stuart kings, and American revolutionaries and later human-rights advocates treated it as a foundation of constitutional liberty, a symbolic meaning far wider than its authors intended.

title: Chronica Majora
creator: matthew-paris
location: Written at St Albans Abbey; autograph manuscripts at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and the British Library
note: Matthew Paris's great chronicle of the world, detailed and opinionated on his own century and illustrated in his own hand.
description: The Chronica Majora begins with the Creation, taking over the chronicle of Roger of Wendover, and from 1236 becomes Matthew Paris's own detailed record of events across Europe and the Mediterranean up to 1259: the reign of Henry III, the conflict between the emperor Frederick II and the papacy, the Mongol invasions and the crusades. Matthew copied many documents into it and wrote outspokenly against royal and papal taxation. Unusually for a chronicler, he illustrated the manuscripts himself with tinted drawings in the margins, including battles, coats of arms, an elephant presented to Henry III and the Mongols, and he made itineraries and maps. The autograph volumes survive at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and in the British Library.

title: Chronicles
creator: froissart
location: Written in the Low Countries, England and France; over 150 manuscripts, many richly illuminated (e.g. the Gruuthuse manuscript, Bibliothèque nationale de France)
note: The great chronicle of the first phase of the Hundred Years' War, celebrating chivalry, battles and pageantry.
description: Froissart's Chronicles, written in French prose in four books, cover events in western Europe from the 1320s to 1400. He began by adapting the chronicle of Jean le Bel and then, by travelling and interviewing participants, extended and repeatedly revised his narrative. The Chronicles contain the classic accounts of the battles of Crécy and Poitiers, the burghers of Calais, the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and the deposition of Richard II. Froissart's outlook is aristocratic and he is often inaccurate on details, but his vividness made him a favourite of nobles, who commissioned splendidly illuminated copies, and of later readers. Lord Berners translated him into English in the 1520s, and he inspired Walter Scott and countless illustrators.

title: History of the Florentine People
creator: bruni
location: Written in Florence
note: Bruni's Latin history of Florence, often called the first modern work of history for its secular, documentary approach.
description: Bruni began his Historiae Florentini populi around 1415 and worked on it until shortly before his death; it runs from the city's founding to 1402. Written in elegant classical Latin modelled on Livy, it rejects the legends of earlier chroniclers about Florence's origins, explains events through human causes rather than divine providence, and draws on documents from the city's archives. Its theme is Florentine liberty, which Bruni traced to the city's foundation under the Roman Republic rather than the empire. The Florentine government granted him tax exemptions for his work, and it was translated into Italian in 1473. It set the pattern for humanist histories of cities and states across Europe.

title: On the Donation of Constantine
creator: valla
location: Written in Naples; first printed 1506, influential edition by Ulrich von Hutten 1518–19
note: Valla's proof, by linguistic and historical analysis, that the document granting the popes power over the West was a forgery.
description: The Donation of Constantine purported to be a decree by which the emperor Constantine, grateful for his cure from leprosy, handed authority over Rome and the western empire to Pope Sylvester I. It had been used to support papal claims since the eleventh century, although its authenticity had been doubted before. Writing in 1440 for his patron Alfonso of Aragon, then at odds with the pope, Valla showed that its Latin contained words and forms unknown in the fourth century, that it contradicted known history, and that no contemporary source mentioned it. The forgery is now generally dated to the eighth century. The treatise circulated in manuscript and was printed by Protestant reformers in the sixteenth century. It is a landmark in the development of historical criticism of sources.

title: The Prince
creator: machiavelli
location: Written at Sant'Andrea in Percussina near Florence; first printed in Rome and Florence, 1532
note: Machiavelli's short, notorious handbook on how new rulers win and keep power, drawn from history and experience.
description: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 in rural exile after the Medici return to Florence, dedicating it eventually to Lorenzo de' Medici in hope of employment. In twenty-six short chapters he classifies principalities, discusses armies, and advises a prince on how to behave, arguing that it is safer to be feared than loved if one cannot be both, and that a ruler must learn to be able not to be good when necessity demands. His examples come from ancient history and from his own experience, especially of Cesare Borgia. The book closes with an appeal to free Italy from the barbarians. Published after his death in 1532, it was placed on the Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Readers have argued ever since over whether it is a cynical manual of tyranny, a satire, or a clear-eyed description of political reality.

title: Discourses on Livy
creator: machiavelli
location: Written in Florence; first printed 1531
note: Machiavelli's commentary on Livy's history of early Rome, the founding text of modern republican political thought.
description: The Discourses on the First Ten Books of Titus Livy, written around 1513–19, use episodes from Livy as starting points for reflections on how republics are founded, how they expand, and how they decay and can be renewed. Machiavelli argued that Rome's conflicts between nobles and people had made it free and powerful rather than weak, that a citizen militia was superior to mercenaries, and that the Roman religion had served the state well. He praised mixed government on Polybius' model. Less famous than The Prince but longer and more systematic, the Discourses were read by English republicans of the seventeenth century, by Montesquieu and by the American founders, and they show the depth of Machiavelli's engagement with history.

title: Florentine Histories
creator: machiavelli
location: Written in Florence for Pope Clement VII; first printed 1532
note: Machiavelli's history of Florence from its origins to 1492, commissioned by the Medici and focused on the causes of civic discord.
description: In 1520 Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, soon to be Pope Clement VII, commissioned Machiavelli to write a history of Florence. He presented the eight completed books to the pope in 1525. Unlike Bruni, Machiavelli was interested less in the city's external glories than in its internal divisions, which he believed had weakened Florence, in contrast to the productive conflicts of ancient Rome. The narrative covers the barbarian invasions, Guelfs and Ghibellines, the revolt of the Ciompi wool workers of 1378, the rise of the Medici, and the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478, ending with the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent in 1492. Writing for Medici patrons, Machiavelli put some of his sharpest judgments into the mouths of historical characters.

title: The History of Italy
creator: guicciardini
location: Written at Arcetri, near Florence; first printed in Florence, 1561
note: Guicciardini's masterpiece on the Italian Wars from 1494 to 1534, which treated Italy as a whole and explained events through politics.
description: Guicciardini wrote the Storia d'Italia in retirement in the last years of his life, revising it repeatedly. It covers the forty years from the French invasion of 1494 to the death of Clement VII in 1534, years in which Italy became the battlefield of France, Spain and the empire and its states lost their independence. He had taken part in many of the events as a diplomat, governor and commander, and he drew on official documents. His explanations are psychological and political, based on the ambitions, fears and miscalculations of rulers, and he often notes how events turned out contrary to expectations. The work was published by his nephew two decades after his death, with some passages critical of the papacy removed, and it was quickly translated into Latin, French and English.

title: A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies
creator: las-casas
location: Written in Spain for Prince Philip; first printed in Seville, 1552
note: Las Casas's searing indictment of Spanish atrocities against Indigenous peoples in the Americas, addressed to the future Philip II.
description: Las Casas wrote the Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias in 1542 for the future Philip II and printed it in Seville in 1552. Region by region, from Hispaniola to Peru, it describes massacres, enslavement, torture and forced labour inflicted on Indigenous peoples by Spanish conquerors and settlers, and it attributes a catastrophic population collapse to their cruelty and greed. Las Casas wrote to persuade the crown to reform colonial policy, and the work contributed to debates that led to the New Laws of 1542. Modern historians accept the reality of widespread atrocity while noting that his figures are often impossible to verify and that epidemic disease caused most deaths. Translated into Dutch, English, French and German, often with lurid engravings by Theodor de Bry, it became a mainstay of anti-Spanish propaganda, the so-called Black Legend.

title: The True History of the Conquest of New Spain
creator: bernal-diaz
location: Written in Santiago de los Caballeros, Guatemala; first printed in Madrid, 1632
note: A conquistador's memoir of Cortés's conquest of the Aztec empire, written decades later from the point of view of the common soldier.
description: Bernal Díaz began writing his Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España in the 1550s and finished a version around 1568, revising it until his death; it was first printed in 1632. He wrote to correct accounts that credited the victory to Cortés alone and to claim recognition for the soldiers who fought alongside him. He describes the landing at Veracruz, the alliance with the Tlaxcalans, the first view of Tenochtitlan, which seemed to the soldiers like an enchanted vision, the meetings with Moctezuma, the Night of Sorrows and the final siege of 1521. He gives a central role to Malinche, the Nahua woman who served as interpreter. The work is an invaluable but partisan source, written from the conquerors' side, and is complemented by Indigenous accounts such as those in the Florentine Codex.

title: Edict of Nantes
creator: henry-iv-of-france
location: Signed at Nantes; original in the Archives nationales, Paris
note: Henry IV's decree granting French Protestants limited freedom of worship and civil rights, ending the Wars of Religion.
description: Henry IV signed the Edict of Nantes in April 1598, after more than three decades of civil war between Catholics and Protestants. It confirmed Catholicism as the state religion but granted the Huguenots freedom of conscience, the right to worship publicly in specified places, access to public office and the universities, special courts, and, in separate articles, the right to hold around a hundred fortified towns. It was a pragmatic compromise rather than a declaration of religious liberty, and it was resented by many Catholics. Louis XIII removed the Protestants' military privileges after the siege of La Rochelle, and Louis XIV revoked the edict entirely in 1685, driving some 200,000 Huguenots into exile across Europe and America.

title: Peace of Westphalia
creator: westphalia-peacemakers
location: Signed at Münster and Osnabrück; originals in national archives, including Vienna, Paris and Stockholm
note: The treaties of Münster and Osnabrück that ended the Thirty Years' War and the Dutch war of independence.
description: The Peace of Westphalia consisted of the treaties signed in 1648 at Osnabrück, between the emperor and Sweden, and at Münster, between the emperor and France, together with the separate Peace of Münster between Spain and the Dutch Republic earlier that year. They ended the Thirty Years' War, which had devastated much of Germany, and the Eighty Years' War, recognising the independence of the Dutch Republic. The treaties confirmed the right of German princes to determine the religion of their territories, now extended to Calvinists, protected religious minorities in some respects, gave territories to France and Sweden, and recognised Swiss independence. Political scientists have often treated Westphalia as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states; many historians argue that this is a later myth, since the treaties strengthened the empire's constitution rather than abolishing it.

title: The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England
creator: clarendon
location: Written in Jersey, France and Montpellier; first printed by the Oxford University Press, 1702–04
note: The royalist statesman Clarendon's classic account of the English Civil War, famous for its character portraits.
description: Clarendon began his History in 1646 while in exile in Jersey, intending it as a confidential account for the king, and resumed it during his second exile after 1667, combining it with his autobiography. It covers the conflict from the accession of Charles I in 1625 to the Restoration of 1660. Clarendon defends the monarchy and the Church of England but criticises the errors of both sides, and his portraits of figures such as Lord Falkland, Hampden and Cromwell are celebrated for their insight and balance. Published by his son in three volumes in 1702–04, at a time of party conflict, it was immediately influential and profitable, its proceeds helping to fund the Clarendon Building in Oxford.

title: Petition of Right
creator: parliament-of-england
location: Parliamentary Archives, Westminster
note: A statement of civil liberties forced on Charles I by Parliament, prohibiting taxation without consent and imprisonment without cause.
description: In 1628 Parliament, led by Sir Edward Coke, Sir John Eliot and others, responded to Charles I's forced loans, arbitrary imprisonment, billeting of soldiers on civilians and use of martial law by drafting a petition reasserting the ancient liberties of the subject, citing Magna Carta and earlier statutes. It declared that no one should be compelled to pay any tax without the consent of Parliament and that no free man should be imprisoned without cause shown. The king reluctantly gave his assent in June 1628 in return for subsidies, but soon disregarded it and ruled without Parliament from 1629 to 1640. The petition is one of the foundational documents of English constitutional law and influenced the American Bill of Rights.

title: Habeas Corpus Act 1679
creator: parliament-of-england
location: Parliamentary Archives, Westminster
note: The English act that strengthened the ancient writ of habeas corpus, protecting people against unlawful detention.
description: The writ of habeas corpus, requiring a jailer to bring a prisoner before a court and justify the detention, had existed in English common law for centuries, but the Crown had found ways to evade it. The Habeas Corpus Act, passed in 1679 under Charles II during the political crisis over the succession, set strict time limits for producing prisoners, imposed penalties on judges and jailers who refused the writ, and forbade sending prisoners overseas to escape the courts' jurisdiction. According to a famous story, it passed the House of Lords only because a fat peer was jokingly counted as ten votes. It became a model for protections against arbitrary detention, and the United States Constitution guarantees the privilege of the writ except in cases of rebellion or invasion.

title: Bill of Rights 1689
creator: parliament-of-england
location: Parliamentary Archives, Westminster
note: The act that settled the Glorious Revolution, limiting royal power and declaring the rights of Parliament and subjects.
description: After James II fled in December 1688 and William of Orange took control, the Convention Parliament drew up a Declaration of Right, read to William and his wife Mary before they accepted the crown in February 1689, and enacted it as the Bill of Rights in December. It listed James's offences and declared illegal the suspending of laws, the levying of taxes and keeping of a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent, and excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments. It asserted free elections, freedom of speech in Parliament, the right to petition the monarch and the right of Protestants to bear arms, and it barred Catholics from the throne. It remains part of the British constitution and was a direct model for parts of the American Bill of Rights, though its protections were for a Protestant political nation rather than universal.

title: The Age of Louis XIV
creator: voltaire
location: Written in France and at Potsdam; first published in Berlin, 1751
note: Voltaire's history of the reign of Louis XIV as an age of civilisation and the arts, not merely of wars and kings.
description: Voltaire worked on Le Siècle de Louis XIV for some twenty years, publishing it in Berlin in 1751 while at the court of Frederick the Great. He declared that he intended to depict not the actions of one man but the spirit of men in the most enlightened age there had ever been. Along with the wars and politics of the reign, the book devotes chapters to government, commerce, law, the church, religious disputes, science, literature and the fine arts, and to anecdotes of court life. Voltaire consulted surviving witnesses and documents. The work admires the king's patronage of culture while condemning religious persecution, including the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. It is a founding work of cultural history.

title: Essay on the Manners and Spirit of Nations
creator: voltaire
location: First published in Geneva, 1756; expanded editions to 1769
note: Voltaire's universal history from Charlemagne to Louis XIII, which began with China and challenged the Christian view of history.
description: The Essai sur les mœurs et l'esprit des nations grew out of Voltaire's wish to give Émilie du Châtelet a history worth reading, and was published in 1756 and repeatedly enlarged. Deliberately answering Bossuet's Discourse on Universal History, which centred on the Jews and Christianity, Voltaire opened with China, India and Persia and the Islamic world before turning to Europe, treating Christianity as one civilisation among others. He was interested in laws, customs, arts and beliefs rather than battles and dynasties, and he relentlessly attacked fanaticism and superstition. Later editions included an introduction he called the Philosophy of History. The work's scope was revolutionary, though its scholarship was uneven and its judgments often polemical.

title: The History of England
creator: hume
location: Written in Edinburgh; published in London
note: Hume's history of England from Julius Caesar to 1688, the standard history for a century and a bestseller.
description: Hume published his History in reverse order, beginning with two volumes on the Stuarts in 1754 and 1756, followed by the Tudors in 1759 and the earlier period in 1762. The first volume was attacked for its sympathy for Charles I and its scepticism about religious enthusiasm on both sides, but the whole became the most popular history of England until Macaulay. Hume argued that English liberty was not an ancient inheritance, as Whig writers claimed, but a recent and somewhat accidental product of conflict, and he gave attention to manners, commerce, learning and the arts. Its elegant prose made it a standard text for generations. Its title page described Hume simply as 'David Hume, Esq.'

title: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
creator: gibbon
location: Written in London and Lausanne; published in London by Strahan and Cadell
note: Gibbon's great narrative of thirteen centuries from the Antonine emperors to the fall of Constantinople.
description: Gibbon published the first volume in 1776 and the last two in 1788, having finished the work in his garden house at Lausanne in June 1787. Its seventy-one chapters run from the empire at its height in the second century to the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453, covering the barbarian invasions, the rise of Christianity, Justinian, Muhammad and the Arab conquests, the crusades and the Mongols. Gibbon combined the critical erudition of antiquarian scholars with the irony and broad view of the Enlightenment, and his footnotes are famously witty. He attributed the fall in part to the triumph of barbarism and religion, and chapters 15 and 16, which treated early Christianity's growth and martyrdoms as human phenomena, provoked furious replies. The work has never been out of print and is regarded as one of the summits of historical writing.

title: Declaration of Independence
creator: jefferson
location: Adopted in Philadelphia; signed engrossed copy in the National Archives, Washington, D.C.
note: The statement adopted by the Continental Congress on 4 July 1776 announcing the independence of the thirteen colonies and asserting natural rights.
description: On 2 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress voted for independence from Britain, and on 4 July it adopted a declaration drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, with edits by John Adams, Benjamin Franklin and the Congress itself, which cut a passage blaming George III for the slave trade. Its preamble states that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that people may alter or abolish a government that destroys these ends. A long list of grievances against the king follows. The engrossed parchment was signed by most delegates on 2 August. The gap between its language of equality and the reality of slavery and the exclusion of women and Native Americans was pointed out from the start, and abolitionists, suffragists and civil-rights leaders invoked it to demand that its promise be fulfilled. It inspired many later declarations of independence.

title: Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
creator: jefferson
location: Drafted in Virginia; enacted by the Virginia General Assembly in Richmond, 1786
note: Jefferson's law disestablishing the Church of England in Virginia and guaranteeing freedom of religious belief.
description: Jefferson drafted the bill in 1777, but it was enacted by the Virginia General Assembly only in January 1786, steered through by James Madison while Jefferson was in France. It declared that no one should be compelled to attend or support any religious worship or suffer for their religious opinions, and that such opinions should not affect civil capacities. Its preamble argued that truth is great and will prevail if left free. The statute ended the established church in Virginia and was a direct precursor of the religion clauses of the First Amendment. Jefferson listed it among the three achievements to be engraved on his tombstone.

title: Constitution of the United States
creator: us-constitutional-convention
location: Signed in Philadelphia; original in the National Archives, Washington, D.C.
note: The world's oldest written national constitution still in force, establishing a federal republic with separated powers.
description: Drafted in secret by the Philadelphia Convention between May and September 1787 and signed on 17 September, the Constitution replaced the Articles of Confederation. Its seven articles create a bicameral Congress, combining equal representation of states in the Senate with representation by population in the House, an executive president chosen by an electoral college, and a federal judiciary, with a system of checks and balances and a division of powers between national and state governments. It included compromises over slavery, including the three-fifths clause and a fugitive slave clause. It came into effect in 1789 after ratification by nine states following fierce debate between Federalists and Anti-Federalists, and it has since been amended twenty-seven times, notably by the Bill of Rights and the post-Civil War amendments that abolished slavery and guaranteed equal protection. Its preamble opens with the words 'We the People'.

title: The Federalist Papers
creator: hamilton
location: Published in New York newspapers; collected edition by J. and A. McLean, New York, 1788
note: Eighty-five essays by Hamilton, Madison and Jay, under the pen name Publius, urging ratification of the Constitution.
description: The Federalist essays appeared in New York newspapers from October 1787 to August 1788 under the pseudonym Publius, to persuade the state to ratify the proposed Constitution. Alexander Hamilton conceived the project and wrote about fifty-one essays, James Madison about twenty-nine and John Jay five; the authorship of a few was long disputed. The essays explain and defend each part of the Constitution. Madison's Federalist No. 10 argues that a large republic can control the effects of faction, and No. 51 that ambition must be made to counteract ambition; Hamilton's No. 78 describes the judiciary as the least dangerous branch. Collected in two volumes in 1788, the essays are still cited by the Supreme Court as evidence of the framers' intentions, and the Anti-Federalist writings that answered them are increasingly studied alongside them.

title: United States Bill of Rights
creator: madison
location: Proposed by Congress in New York; original enrolled copy in the National Archives, Washington, D.C.
note: The first ten amendments to the US Constitution, guaranteeing freedoms of religion, speech, press and assembly and rights of the accused.
description: Many opponents of the Constitution demanded a bill of rights, and several states ratified only on the understanding that one would follow. In June 1789 James Madison, drawing on the Virginia Declaration of Rights and the proposals of the state conventions, introduced amendments in the first Congress. Congress sent twelve to the states in September 1789, and ten were ratified by December 1791. They protect freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition, the right to keep and bear arms, protection against unreasonable searches, the rights to due process, a speedy and public jury trial and counsel, and freedom from cruel and unusual punishment, and they reserve other powers to the states or the people. Originally they restrained only the federal government; after the Fourteenth Amendment the Supreme Court gradually applied most of them to the states.

title: Common Sense
creator: paine
location: First printed in Philadelphia by Robert Bell, January 1776
note: Paine's best-selling pamphlet that made the case for American independence and against hereditary monarchy in plain language.
description: Published anonymously in Philadelphia in January 1776, when most colonists still hoped for reconciliation with Britain, Common Sense argued that it was absurd for an island to rule a continent, that monarchy and hereditary succession were irrational and corrupt, and that the colonies should declare independence and form a republic. Paine wrote in direct, vigorous prose, avoiding Latin quotations and appealing to ordinary readers. It sold in huge numbers, with estimates often given in the tens or hundreds of thousands, a debated figure, and it was read aloud in taverns and camps. It is credited with shifting public opinion towards independence in the months before July 1776.

title: Rights of Man
creator: paine
location: Published in London by J. S. Jordan
note: Paine's reply to Burke, defending the French Revolution and arguing that every generation has the right to choose its government.
description: Paine published the first part of Rights of Man in March 1791 in answer to Burke's Reflections. He argued that rights derive from nature, not from inherited institutions, that the living cannot be bound by the dead, and that hereditary government is a form of usurpation. In the second part, published in 1792, he proposed a programme of social reform funded by progressive taxation, including support for the poor, old-age pensions and public education. The work sold widely among artisans and working people, and the British government charged Paine with seditious libel; he was convicted in absence and outlawed. It is a classic of democratic radicalism.

title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
creator: burke
location: Published in London by J. Dodsley, November 1790
note: Burke's attack on the principles of the French Revolution and defence of tradition and gradual reform, the founding text of modern conservatism.
description: Written as a letter to a young Frenchman and published in November 1790, before the Terror, the Reflections responded to a sermon by the Dissenting minister Richard Price praising the Revolution. Burke argued that the revolutionaries' abstract theories of rights would destroy the institutions, customs and habits of deference that held society together, and predicted that the Revolution would lead to anarchy and military dictatorship. He contrasted it with the English Revolution of 1688, which he presented as a preservation of ancient liberties. His lament for Marie Antoinette and the passing of the age of chivalry became famous. The book sold widely and provoked many replies, including Paine's Rights of Man and Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Men. It remains central to debates about reform and revolution.

title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
creator: french-national-assembly
location: Adopted at Versailles, 26 August 1789; original in the Archives nationales, Paris
note: The French revolutionary declaration of natural and civil rights, adopted in August 1789, a cornerstone of modern human-rights law.
description: The National Constituent Assembly adopted the Declaration on 26 August 1789, after the abolition of feudal privileges, as a preamble to the constitution it was preparing. Its seventeen articles proclaim that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, that the aim of political association is the preservation of the natural rights of liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression, and that sovereignty resides in the nation. It establishes the principles of law as the expression of the general will, equality before the law, presumption of innocence, freedom of opinion, including religious opinion, and of expression, and the separation of powers. Influenced by Enlightenment thought and by American declarations, it did not extend political rights to women or address slavery, omissions challenged at the time by Olympe de Gouges and by abolitionists. It remains part of the French constitution.

title: Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen
creator: olympe-de-gouges
location: Published in Paris, September 1791
note: Olympe de Gouges's article-by-article rewriting of the 1789 Declaration to include women.
description: In September 1791, as the new constitution was completed, Olympe de Gouges published a pamphlet addressed to Queen Marie Antoinette that rewrote the Declaration of the Rights of Man article by article to apply to women. Its first article declares that woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights. Its tenth article notes that if women have the right to mount the scaffold, they must also have the right to mount the rostrum. She called for equal rights to property and public employment, the right of unmarried mothers to name the fathers of their children, and a new social contract for marriage. The pamphlet had little impact at the time, and its author was guillotined in 1793, but it has become a classic text of feminism.

title: Haitian Declaration of Independence
creator: dessalines
location: Proclaimed at Gonaïves, 1 January 1804; only known original printed copy in The National Archives, Kew
note: The proclamation of the independence of Haiti, the first state founded by people who had freed themselves from slavery.
description: On 1 January 1804, at Gonaïves, Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the independence of the former French colony of Saint-Domingue under the Taíno name Haiti. The declaration, written by his secretary Louis Boisrond-Tonnerre, addresses the people of Haiti and urges them to renounce France forever and to defend their liberty to the death, recalling the cruelty of French rule and of Napoleon's attempt to restore slavery. It followed thirteen years of revolution that began with the slave uprising of 1791. Haiti became the second independent republic in the Americas and the first in Latin America, but France and other powers were slow to recognise it, and in 1825 France imposed a crippling indemnity. In 2010 the historian Julia Gaffield found a printed copy of the declaration in the British National Archives, the only known original printing.

title: History of France
creator: michelet
location: Written in Paris; published by Hachette and others
note: Michelet's vast, passionate history of France from its origins to the Revolution, centred on the life of the people.
description: Michelet published the first six volumes of his Histoire de France, on the Middle Ages, between 1833 and 1844, using his privileged access to the National Archives. He then interrupted it to write his History of the French Revolution (1847–53), and returned to complete the story from the Renaissance to 1789 in eleven more volumes, finished in 1867. His famous 'Tableau de la France' describes the regions of the country as a living landscape, and his portrait of Joan of Arc as a saint of the people became a national icon. The volumes on the sixteenth century popularised the word Renaissance for the age of rediscovery of the world and of man. Later volumes are more anticlerical and polemical. Michelet's ambition was to resurrect the whole life of the past.

title: The History of England from the Accession of James the Second
creator: macaulay
location: Written in London; published by Longman
note: Macaulay's vivid, Whiggish history of the Glorious Revolution and its aftermath, one of the bestselling histories ever written.
description: Macaulay originally planned to carry his history from 1685 to the early nineteenth century, but he managed only the reigns of James II and William III; the fifth volume, edited by his sister, appeared after his death in 1859. The famous third chapter surveys the state of England in 1685, its population, roads, towns and social classes, an early attempt at social history. The narrative portrays James II as a would-be absolutist and William III as the deliverer of English liberties, and the Revolution of 1688 as the foundation of national greatness. The first two volumes sold tens of thousands of copies in Britain and many more in America. It is the classic example of what Butterfield later criticised as the Whig interpretation of history.

title: The French Revolution: A History
creator: carlyle
location: Written in Chelsea, London; published by James Fraser
note: Carlyle's visionary, present-tense narrative of the French Revolution, rewritten after the first manuscript was burned.
description: Carlyle's French Revolution, in three volumes titled The Bastille, The Constitution and The Guillotine, covers events from the death of Louis XV in 1774 to Napoleon's 'whiff of grapeshot' in 1795. In March 1835 the only manuscript of the first volume was accidentally burned at the house of John Stuart Mill, to whom he had lent it, and Carlyle rewrote it from memory. Written largely in the present tense, with exclamations, prophecies and addresses to the characters, it presents the Revolution as a fiery judgment on a decayed aristocratic order. It made Carlyle famous, influenced Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities and remains a literary classic, though not a reliable guide to the facts.

title: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
creator: carlyle
location: Delivered in London, 1840; published by James Fraser, 1841
note: Six lectures in which Carlyle argued that history is the biography of great men.
description: In May 1840 Carlyle gave six public lectures in London on the hero as divinity (Odin), prophet (Muhammad), poet (Dante and Shakespeare), priest (Luther and Knox), man of letters (Johnson, Rousseau and Burns) and king (Cromwell and Napoleon). He declared that universal history is at bottom the history of the great men who have worked here. His sympathetic treatment of Muhammad was unusual in Britain at the time. The lectures were enormously popular and gave a name to the 'great man theory' of history, which Herbert Spencer and others criticised for ignoring the social conditions that produce great individuals. Carlyle's later glorification of strong rulers has made the book controversial.

title: Democracy in America
creator: tocqueville
location: Written in Paris after travels in the United States in 1831–32; published by Gosselin
note: Tocqueville's classic study of American democracy as a new social condition of equality and what it meant for liberty.
description: After nine months in the United States in 1831–32, Tocqueville published the first volume of De la démocratie en Amérique in 1835 and the second in 1840. The first describes American institutions: townships, federalism, the courts, the press, parties and the power of the majority, which he feared could become a new kind of tyranny. It ends with a long chapter on the three races of America, analysing the destruction of Native Americans and slavery, which he predicted would lead to catastrophe. The second volume asks how equality of conditions shapes ideas, feelings and manners, warning of individualism and of a mild despotism of administration, and praising voluntary associations, local liberty and religion as counterweights. It is still read as the most perceptive book ever written about the United States.

title: The Old Regime and the Revolution
creator: tocqueville
location: Written in Paris and Tours; published by Michel Lévy
note: Tocqueville's archival study arguing that the French Revolution completed the centralisation begun by the monarchy.
description: In L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution Tocqueville used provincial archives, especially those of the intendants, to study France before 1789. He argued that the Revolution was less a break than a continuation of trends, above all the centralisation of administration under the absolute monarchy, which had already deprived the nobility of its political role while leaving its privileges, making them hated. He observed that revolutions tend to come not when conditions are at their worst but when a bad government begins to reform. The book was planned as the first part of a larger work that his death prevented. It is a pioneering example of archival social and administrative history.

title: Declaration of Sentiments
creator: stanton
location: Adopted at the Seneca Falls Convention, New York, July 1848
note: The founding manifesto of the American women's rights movement, modelled on the Declaration of Independence.
description: The Declaration of Sentiments, drafted mainly by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, was adopted at the first women's rights convention, held at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, on 19–20 July 1848. Deliberately echoing the Declaration of Independence, it declared that all men and women are created equal, and listed the injuries inflicted on women: denial of the vote, of property rights for married women, of education and professions, and of equality in church and law. It was followed by resolutions, of which the demand for the vote was the most controversial and passed only after Frederick Douglass spoke in support. It was signed by sixty-eight women and thirty-two men. The convention launched the organised movement that eventually won women's suffrage.

title: The Communist Manifesto
creator: marx
location: Written in Brussels with Friedrich Engels; first printed in London, February 1848
note: Marx and Engels's short programme for the Communist League, which presents history as the history of class struggles.
description: The Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei was commissioned by the Communist League, a small group of German émigré workers, and written by Marx with Friedrich Engels in Brussels at the turn of 1847–48; it was printed in London in February 1848, just as revolution broke out across Europe. It opens by declaring that a spectre is haunting Europe and that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. It describes the bourgeoisie as a revolutionary class that has transformed the world through capitalism, and predicts that the proletariat it has created will overthrow it, abolishing private property in the means of production. It ends with a call for workers of all countries to unite. Little noticed at first, it became one of the most widely read political documents in history, and it is admired by some and condemned by others for what was done in its name.

title: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte
creator: marx
location: Written in London; first published in New York in the journal Die Revolution
note: Marx's analysis of the coup by Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte in 1851, opening with the remark that history repeats itself, first as tragedy, then as farce.
description: Written between December 1851 and March 1852, immediately after Louis-Napoleon's coup d'état, this essay analyses the French revolution of 1848 and its collapse into a new Bonapartist dictatorship. Marx famously observes that men make their own history, but not under circumstances of their own choosing, and that history happens twice, the first time as tragedy, the second as farce. He traces the shifting alliances of classes and parties and explains how Louis-Napoleon could rise by balancing between them, with the support of the small-holding peasantry. It is considered his most brilliant piece of historical writing and a classic of political analysis.

title: Emancipation Proclamation
creator: lincoln
location: Signed in Washington, D.C., 1 January 1863; original in the National Archives
note: Lincoln's wartime order declaring enslaved people in the rebelling Confederate states to be free.
description: Lincoln issued a preliminary proclamation after the battle of Antietam in September 1862 and signed the final proclamation on 1 January 1863. Issued as a war measure under his powers as commander-in-chief, it declared that all persons held as slaves in areas then in rebellion against the United States were and henceforward shall be free. It did not apply to slave states loyal to the Union or to Union-occupied areas, so it freed few people immediately, but every advance of Union armies thereafter brought freedom, and it authorised the enlistment of Black soldiers, nearly 200,000 of whom served. It transformed the war into a war against slavery and deterred European recognition of the Confederacy. Slavery was abolished throughout the United States by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865.

title: Gettysburg Address
creator: lincoln
location: Delivered at the Soldiers' National Cemetery, Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, 19 November 1863; five autograph copies survive, including in the Library of Congress
note: Lincoln's 272-word speech at Gettysburg redefining the Civil War as a struggle for equality and government by the people.
description: Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the national cemetery at Gettysburg, four and a half months after the battle, following a two-hour oration by Edward Everett. In about two minutes he recalled that the nation had been conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal, said that the living could not consecrate the ground that the dead had already hallowed, and called for a new birth of freedom so that government of the people, by the people, for the people shall not perish from the earth. Newspaper reactions divided along party lines. Five manuscript copies in Lincoln's hand survive, which differ slightly; the Bliss copy is the one usually reproduced. The address became one of the most quoted speeches in history.

title: Histories of the Latin and Germanic Peoples, 1494–1514
creator: ranke
location: Published in Leipzig and Berlin by Reimer
note: Ranke's first book, whose preface set out the programme of showing the past 'as it actually was'.
description: Ranke's Geschichten der romanischen und germanischen Völker von 1494 bis 1514 described the struggles over Italy at the beginning of the Italian Wars, treating the Latin and Germanic nations as a single cultural unit. In a famous preface he wrote that history had been assigned the office of judging the past and instructing the present for the benefit of future ages, but that his work aspired only to show what actually happened. In an appendix, published as a separate volume, he subjected earlier historians, including Guicciardini, to rigorous criticism, arguing that only contemporary documents and eyewitness reports could be trusted. The book earned him a chair at Berlin and set out the method of critical history.

title: The History of the Popes
creator: ranke
location: Published in Berlin; based on research in Venetian and Roman archives
note: Ranke's study of the papacy in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, praised for its impartiality by Protestant and Catholic readers.
description: Die römischen Päpste, ihre Kirche und ihr Staat im sechzehnten und siebzehnten Jahrhundert was based on Ranke's research in Venice, Vienna and Rome, where the Vatican archives were closed to him, so he relied on the reports of Venetian ambassadors and on private collections. It describes the Catholic Reformation and the papacy as a political power during the age of the Reformation and the Counter-Reformation. Though a Lutheran, Ranke wrote without polemic, which was widely admired, though the book was placed on the Catholic Index. Macaulay's essay on it popularised it in England. It is a classic example of Ranke's cool, document-based narrative of states and churches.

title: History of Rome
creator: mommsen
location: Written in Zurich and Breslau; published in Leipzig and Berlin
note: Mommsen's vivid, politically charged history of the Roman Republic, cited when he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1902.
description: The first three volumes of Mommsen's Römische Geschichte, published in 1854–56, cover Rome from its origins to Caesar's victory at Thapsus in 46 BC. Mommsen wrote with the energy of a political pamphleteer, treating the Roman aristocracy as a decadent oligarchy and Caesar as a genius who created a new order; he described the politics of the Republic in the vocabulary of nineteenth-century parties.
